### Simulation with known truth {#sec-sim-design}

Comparisons with published estimates (@sec-measures) cannot show whether a
method's uncertainty is right: the published values are themselves estimates,
and the held-out estimates share the constraints' sample, so their errors are
correlated. We therefore also evaluate the methods where the truth is known.
For PUMA 4701502 we took 50 populations as truths: 25 draws of the reference
posterior at $\alpha = 0.01$, each made an integer population by one
multinomial draw of the PUMA's households and group-quarters persons, and 25
IPF multinomial draws. The first kind of truth shares the model's structure;
the second does not, and is the case most favourable to IPF.

From each truth we drew a survey, keeping each household and group-quarters
person independently with probability 1/8, and estimated every published cell
from the sampled records' weights. Each survey was refitted to a reduced set of
constraints: B01001, B03002, B08301, B25003 and C24010 at block group and tract,
less the 26 finest occupation lines of C24010, and B17024 and B26001 at tract
(141 block group and 273 tract cells). B19001 and B23001 were left unfitted, and
the six held-out tables remained held out. The refits use the published
covariance $\Sigma$, scaled by one constant per kind of truth so that its
diagonal matches the survey's sampling variance in the median constraint cell
($c = 0.40$ for the posterior truths and [UPDATE: calibration.json,
ipf_multinomial c] for the IPF truths); its correlations are kept. IPF, IPF
multinomial, VB Gaussian and short HMC were refitted to every survey, at
$\alpha = 0.01$. We keep 16 draws per method and truth: for short HMC, one from
each of its 16 superchains (256 chains in all); a short HMC refit took a median
of 6.4 minutes of sampling. So that every method is compared with the integer
truths on equal terms, each VB and HMC draw is made an integer population by
one multinomial draw, as the IPF multinomial draws are.

We measure calibration by the rank of the true count among a method's 16 draws,
from 0 (below every draw) to 16 (above every draw), with ties broken at random
[@hamill2001; @talts2018]. If the draws and the truth came from one
distribution, every rank would be equally likely, each with probability 1/17;
draws that are too narrow put the truth at the extreme ranks, and a biased
method tilts the histogram. We measure accuracy by the absolute error of the
point estimate (IPF's fit; the mean of the other methods' draws) and by the
continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of the draws [@gneiting2007], which
rewards draws that are both centred on the truth and no wider than necessary,
and equals the absolute error for a point estimate. Both are in units of the
cell's standard error.

### Calibration against known truth {#sec-sim-results}

@fig-sim gives the result. On the held-out tables, which none of the refits saw,
the short HMC posterior is close to calibrated: the true count is about equally
likely to fall at any rank among its draws, and it falls outside all 16 of them
in [UPDATE: ranks.csv, hmc_short_int, block group, heldout, all, ranks 0 + 16]
of cells against a nominal 12 percent. The IPF multinomial draws are not
calibrated: the true count falls outside all 16 of them in [UPDATE: ranks.csv,
ipf_multinomial, ranks 0 + 16, both kinds] of held-out cells. Their spread is
only multinomial noise around a single allocation, which has absorbed the
survey's sampling error rather than expressed it. This holds when the truth is
itself an IPF multinomial draw, the case most favourable to IPF. VB Gaussian
lies between the two: its histogram slopes upward, so it tends to underestimate
the held-out counts. When the truth is an IPF draw, short HMC shows an excess of
cells whose truth lies below every draw ([UPDATE: ranks.csv, hmc_short_int,
ipf_multinomial truths, rank 0]); [UPDATE: confirm from the truth_zero rows of
ranks.csv that these are mostly zero truths, which IPF enforces exactly and the
model does not].

The methods differ far less in point accuracy than in calibration. IPF's single
fit is slightly the most accurate point estimate (median absolute error of
[UPDATE: summary.csv, ipf_abs_error_p50, heldout, nonzero] standard errors,
against [UPDATE: hmc_short_int_abs_error_p50] for the mean of the short HMC
draws), while the short HMC draws have the lowest CRPS of any method, for both
kinds of truth ([UPDATE: summary.csv, *_crps]; Table S[UPDATE]). The posterior
therefore buys little in point accuracy over raking. What it buys is an
uncertainty statement that can be trusted on tables it was not fitted to, which
the multinomial replicates of IPF do not provide.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.48
#| fig-height: 5.9
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Calibration and accuracy against known truth (@sec-sim-design). Fifty
#|   populations of PUMA 4701502 serve as truths: 25 draws of the reference
#|   posterior (upper row of the top panels) and 25 IPF multinomial draws (lower
#|   row). Each was surveyed by Bernoulli sampling of 1 in 8 households and
#|   group-quarters persons and refitted, at $\alpha = 0.01$, to a reduced set
#|   of constraints. Top: for every block group cell of the six held-out tables,
#|   the rank of the true count among the method's 16 draws, from 0 (below every
#|   draw) to 16 (above every draw), ties broken at random. A calibrated method
#|   gives every rank equally often (dashed line, 1/17); a U shape means the
#|   draws are too narrow, a slope that they are biased. Bottom: the median
#|   absolute error of the point estimate (IPF's single fit; the mean of the
#|   other methods' draws) and the mean continuous ranked probability score of
#|   the draws, over the held-out cells whose true count is not zero, in units
#|   of the cell's standard error; lower is better. All draws are integer
#|   populations: VB's and HMC's are made so by one multinomial draw each, as
#|   IPF's multinomial draws and the truths are.
source("sim/fig_sim.R")
plot_sim(sim_data("sim"))
```
